rows.evidence: Q1: Material and Methods, Experiments 1-4 and Tables 8-17 <U+2013> own three-year field plot experiments (2012-2016) on rice and soybean at the Ushkonyr site, south-east Kazakhstan. Q2: Abstract and Conclusions (first bullet) <U+2013> the authors state as their own finding that drip irrigation with mulching film promotes early and uniform emergence of rice and soybean shoots and intensive plant growth; Methods list field seed viability counts on fixed 0.25 m2 platforms at full emergence and phenological observations.
rows.notes: The emergence result is stated only in the abstract/conclusions; no table or figure with emergence or seedling counts is presented, so the support is a narrative assertion from the authors' own trials. The claimed technology (drip + plastic mulch film) matches. Q3: only one observation method. Q4: no soil temperature or moisture under the film measured as the mechanism; the 'film keeps heat and moisture' statement is asserted, not measured. Q5: single site, one soil; two crops only. Q6: plots of 14-50 m2. Q7: no stated requirement for emergence effect beyond generic claims that the film is 'a necessity' in a variable climate. Q8: small plot size mentioned as a cost-driven design constraint but not presented as a limitation of the emergence result. Q9: no dispersion for emergence.

rows.evidence: Q1: Material and Methods, Experiments 1-4, Tables 8-17 <U+2013> own multi-year field plot experiments on rice and soybean. Q2: Results (text after Table 12/Table 13) and Conclusions <U+2013> drip irrigation with mulching film reduced weed infestation of rice 8-10 times, allowing manual, mechanical and chemical weed control to be dropped; drip plots without film were overrun with weeds and chemical/mechanical control was ineffective, so they were excluded; for soybean, drip under mulch film was the most effective weed control with no more than 36-44 weeds/m2 in the early season; weed counts made by the standard national monitoring technique.
rows.notes: Weed suppression is reported as the study's own result, but attributed by the authors to the mulching film rather than to localized wetting by drip as the passage states; drip without film actually increased weed problems. No weed-count table is presented; figures are narrative. Q3: single counting method. Q4: localized soil wetting not measured as the mechanism. Q5: one site/soil, two crops. Q6: plot scale only. Q7: the necessity of the mulch film is a component of the technology itself rather than an external support condition; treated as 'no'. Q8: no limitation stated for the weed result. Q9: '8-10 times' and '36-44 units/m2' are approximate ranges across variants, not dispersion statistics.

notes: Full text appears complete. The paper is a poorly structured, partly machine-translated report; several results (emergence, weed counts, nutrient regime) are asserted in text/conclusions without supporting tables. Yield tables give HCP0.95 (LSD) values but no dispersion for the claimed effects. Table 17 gives <U+00B1>m for soybean yield components by cultivar but not for a mulch comparison.
